newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bombers confront Netanyahu in Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Bombers confront Netanyahu in Jerusalem.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu promised to protect Israelis from Palestinian suicide bombers when elected prime minister 14 months ago.
On Wednesday they proved him wrong.
Two human bombs ripped up a Jewish street market in the heart of Jerusalem, posing a deadly challenge to the 47-year-old leader's pledge to provide peace with security.

Everyone -- from political analysts to people on the street -- was asking whether he could answer the suicide bombings any better than the Labour party predecessors he accused of being soft on terrorism.
Politicians and analysts alike forecast that in time he and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat would have to get back to the negotiating table.
Israeli President Ezer Weizman said the ultimate solution to the violence was an enduring peace agreement.
"Unless we have peace, it won't stop," Weizman said.
When pushed to the wall, even Netanyahu's senior aide Danny Naveh declined to spell out for reporters how this government would confront the issue differently.
"I personally don't think he has a different option," said Mark Heller, senior research associate at Tel Aviv University's Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies.
"When in the past he was asked what he would do instead, there was never a compelling answer," Heller told Reuters.
As with every prime minister in the most recent past, the right-wing Likud party leader ordered all Palestinians back to the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
Like his Labour party predecessors Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres, he demanded that Arafat crack down on militant groups suspected of launching the attack.
And as in a previous wave of attacks under Labour, Arafat ordered the arrests.
Some analysts suggested Netanyahu might try to send Israeli soldiers into Palestinian-ruled areas to do what he believed Arafat could not.
But politicians said this would run against the advice of an Israeli security establishment which believes it would trigger an even more violent response.
"Netanyahu today is in the same position as Rabin and will respond exactly the same," said Shimon Shiffer, diplomatic correspondent for the best-selling newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
"The difference is that he promised not to negotiate if the terrorism continued. But in fact the previous government didn't do it either the moment there was terrorism," he said.
"In the end it's the same history, the same Israel, and the same government and there won't be any difference."
"All of the mediators will get involved...It won't stop," Shiffer said.
Labour party leader Ehud Barak, an ex-army chief who is Netanyahu's most formidable challenger, said the attack proved Israel's enemies didn't distinguish one government from another.

"I fought for decades in uniform against terrorism and I never found that beyond the desire to kill Jews, the terrorists were interested in the question of which political party was in government," Barak told Israel's Channel One television.
In Netanyahu's case, peacemaking is already largely at a standstill, mostly because of Jewish settlement expansion. Intelligence-sharing is next to nil.
Israeli philosopher Meron Benvinisti, a veteran student of the Arab-Jewish conflict, said Netanyahu's demands that Arafat crack down were not what counted.
"Arafat has to do more. But that is something that Arafat must decide because Arafat is not his (Netanyahu's) policeman, he is not under his orders," Benvinisti told Reuters.
Shiffer, the journalist, said in the end the question was whether President Bill Clinton was ready to take a get-tough approach with Palestinians and cut U.S. aid to them.
"He is the only person who can really affect what is happening here -- nobody else," Shiffer said.
